title: Teach me
hook: a warrior drops his bow, says "teach me," and falls silent: where the Gita's teaching begins
carry: the teaching begins when the student says "teach me"
tomorrow: your right is to the work. so do results matter at all?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the blind king's word, mamakah, mine, set his sons against his nephews: peace comes without "I" and "mine." Today, out on the field, one of those nephews drops his bow.

The conch shells have sounded. Arjuna, the finest archer on the field, asks Krishna, his friend and charioteer, to drive between the two armies so he can see who he's fighting. He sees teachers. Uncles. Cousins. Friends. His bow slips from his hand. His mouth goes dry. He sits down in the chariot, and his eyes fill with tears. Then he says something a warrior almost never says out loud.
screen: `BETWEEN THE TWO ARMIES.` → `TEACHERS, UNCLES, COUSINS.` → `THE BOW SLIPS.`

segments.voice: He turns to Krishna and says: my mind is confused about dharma. Tell me plainly what is better. shishyas te 'ham shadhi mam tvam prapannam: I am your student; teach me, I take refuge in you. Then Sanjaya, the narrator, reports his last words before the teaching: na yotsya, I will not fight. And then a tiny word: iti. Thus. Sanskrit has no quotation marks; iti does the job, closing someone's words. After it, Sanjaya's voice: and having said that, he fell silent. Hold that silence. Krishna, the text says, answers as if smiling, and the teaching of the Gita begins; most of its seven hundred verses are Krishna's. Notice the order. Krishna doesn't lecture a warrior who's sure of himself. The teaching starts when Arjuna stops, admits he's lost, and asks. This is the oldest shape of Hindu learning: guru and shishya, teacher and student. Later in the Gita, Krishna says it outright: learn by bowing, by asking questions, by serving, and those who have seen the truth will teach you. That's why students touch a teacher's feet before a lesson, why many classes open with om saha navavatu, may it protect us both, teacher and student together, and why Guru Purnima is a day for thanking teachers. And iti marks the exact spot: where Arjuna's voice stops, the teaching starts. In this tradition, saying I don't know, teach me, isn't a weakness. It's the door.
screen: `I AM YOUR STUDENT. TEACH ME.` · `NA YOTSYA, ITI: HE FELL SILENT.` · `THEN KRISHNA SPEAKS.` · `BOW, ASK, SERVE.` · then, large: `WHERE HIS VOICE STOPS, THE TEACHING STARTS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person who taught you something real: a grandparent, a coach, a teacher. If you pray, fold your hands and bow your head to them, the way students bow before a lesson; you might say om saha navavatu, may it protect us both. If you don't pray, just name silently what they taught you, and say thank you. Then rest with the breath.
Two hundred core words. Today, iti, thus: the tiny word that closes Arjuna's na yotsya, and opens the space where the teaching begins. And shishya, student: what Arjuna calls himself.
The line for today: the teaching begins when the student says "teach me." Until tomorrow.
